scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that passion for ordinary things sparks ideas, then argues great ideas also come from rare problems; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Some of the greatest inventions began with someone wondering about an everyday thing.
Some people argue that the best ideas arise from a passionate interest in commonplace things.
I agree that passion for ordinary things often sparks great ideas, but I do not believe this is their only source.

sections.role: Body 1 — Why everyday passion sparks ideas

sentences.text: First, a deep interest in ordinary things really can lead to remarkable ideas.
People who study everyday objects closely often notice what others overlook.
For example, the simple sight of an apple falling is said to have led Newton toward the idea of gravity.
This shows that great discoveries can grow from curiosity about the most common things.
Everyday problems, such as how to keep food fresh, have inspired countless useful inventions.
Passion turns ordinary curiosity into the patient effort that real discovery demands.
To this extent, the statement captures a genuine truth about creativity.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why rare problems matter too

sentences.text: Second, however, many of the best ideas come from rare or difficult problems, not commonplace ones.
Great breakthroughs often arise from questions far removed from ordinary daily life.
Consider the abstract puzzles of mathematics or space that have reshaped how we understand the universe.
Such ideas show that passion can attach to the unusual and the abstract as well as the everyday.
Some discoveries also come from teamwork, accident, or careful study rather than a single personal interest.
What matters most is genuine passion, whatever its subject happens to be.
Great ideas, then, can spring from the rare just as easily as from the commonplace.
In conclusion, a passionate interest in everyday things truly can produce wonderful ideas.
But the best ideas also arise from rare problems, abstract questions, and many other sources.
What unites great ideas is not commonplace subject matter but the passion behind the search.
